retrieved_chunks.title: Upstream request timeouts
retrieved_chunks.text:
Upstream request timeouts
Scope: Application HTTP clients exceeding configured deadlines
## Symptoms
ReadTimeout; ConnectTimeout; upstream request timed out; 504.

These are project-authored investigation notes, not an official diagnosis. Use the supplied logs to establish observed symptoms and cite their original line identifiers. Treat configuration changes, impact and the exact root cause as unknown unless evidence supports them. This runbook suggests checks; CloudLens never executes changes to the affected system.


## Diagnostic checks
Identify whether the timeout occurred while connecting, reading, writing or waiting for a connection pool slot. Compare client and upstream request IDs, timestamps and configured timeouts. Inspect upstream latency, availability and dependency metrics. Check network reachability for connection timeouts and response behavior for read timeouts. Repeated timeouts alone do not establish CPU overload, traffic volume or memory pressure. Collect metrics before ranking those explanations.


## Missing evidence
Collect surrounding application logs, relevant deployment configuration, dependency-side evidence and a known-good comparison. Preserve timestamps when present and label absent timestamps as unknown. Record evidence that contradicts a proposed cause as well as evidence supporting it. If only a generic failure message is available, report insufficient evidence and request context rather than asserting a cause.


## Recovery guidance
Address a verified upstream or connectivity issue through its owner. Adjust deadlines only after measuring normal latency and reviewing user impact. Bound retries and use backoff for transient failures; avoid multiplying load with unlimited retry loops. Verify successful requests, acceptable latency and fewer timeout errors under a representative workload.

retrieved_chunks.title: Reverse proxy gateway errors
retrieved_chunks.text:
Reverse proxy gateway errors
Scope: Nginx reporting failed upstream connections or responses
## Symptoms
502 Bad Gateway; 504 Gateway Timeout; upstream prematurely closed connection.

These are project-authored investigation notes, not an official diagnosis. Use the supplied logs to establish observed symptoms and cite their original line identifiers. Treat configuration changes, impact and the exact root cause as unknown unless evidence supports them. This runbook suggests checks; CloudLens never executes changes to the affected system.


## Diagnostic checks
Compare proxy and application timestamps and request identifiers. Check the configured upstream host and port, process health and listening interface. Distinguish connection refusal, upstream closure and response timeout in proxy error logs. Inspect relevant connection and read timeout settings. A proxy 502 does not uniquely identify an application crash; incorrect upstream configuration can produce a similar symptom.


## Missing evidence
Collect surrounding application logs, relevant deployment configuration, dependency-side evidence and a known-good comparison. Preserve timestamps when present and label absent timestamps as unknown. Record evidence that contradicts a proposed cause as well as evidence supporting it. If only a generic failure message is available, report insufficient evidence and request context rather than asserting a cause.


## Recovery guidance
Correct the confirmed upstream address or application issue using the approved deployment process. Review timeout changes against measured behavior rather than simply increasing every limit. Validate proxy configuration before reloading. Verify the proxied endpoint, application health and an end-to-end request, and monitor for recurring gateway failures.

retrieved_chunks.title: External API throttling
retrieved_chunks.text:
External API throttling
Scope: Dependencies limiting request rates or returning transient overload
## Symptoms
TooManyRequests; ThrottlingException; 429; rate limit exceeded.

These are project-authored investigation notes, not an official diagnosis. Use the supplied logs to establish observed symptoms and cite their original line identifiers. Treat configuration changes, impact and the exact root cause as unknown unless evidence supports them. This runbook suggests checks; CloudLens never executes changes to the affected system.


## Diagnostic checks
Identify the dependency, operation and throttling response. Inspect retry headers where provided, SDK retry configuration and total request attempts. Compare concurrency and request rates against documented limits. Separate throttling from authentication failures and persistent validation errors. Retrying all errors indiscriminately can amplify load. The supplied logs may show throttling without establishing how much traffic caused it.


## Missing evidence
Collect surrounding application logs, relevant deployment configuration, dependency-side evidence and a known-good comparison. Preserve timestamps when present and label absent timestamps as unknown. Record evidence that contradicts a proposed cause as well as evidence supporting it. If only a generic failure message is available, report insufficient evidence and request context rather than asserting a cause.


## Recovery guidance
Reduce verified concurrency or request frequency and use bounded retries with backoff and jitter. Cache suitable repeated work. Request quota changes only through the resource owner when justified. Verify that successful calls recover while total attempts remain bounded, and retain a clear failure message when the retry budget is exhausted.

retrieved_chunks.title: Database reachability failures
retrieved_chunks.text:
Database reachability failures
Scope: Database connections refused, unreachable or timing out
## Symptoms
connection refused; connection timed out; could not translate host name.

These are project-authored investigation notes, not an official diagnosis. Use the supplied logs to establish observed symptoms and cite their original line identifiers. Treat configuration changes, impact and the exact root cause as unknown unless evidence supports them. This runbook suggests checks; CloudLens never executes changes to the affected system.


## Diagnostic checks
Distinguish DNS failure, connection refusal, network timeout and database authentication rejection. Confirm the intended endpoint and port from configuration without showing credentials. Test DNS and TCP reachability from the same network as the application. Inspect database availability, routing, security groups and network ACLs with the resource owner. Compare timestamps with maintenance events. A refused connection and a timed-out connection suggest different checks; neither proves a security group fault.


## Missing evidence
Collect surrounding application logs, relevant deployment configuration, dependency-side evidence and a known-good comparison. Preserve timestamps when present and label absent timestamps as unknown. Record evidence that contradicts a proposed cause as well as evidence supporting it. If only a generic failure message is available, report insufficient evidence and request context rather than asserting a cause.


## Recovery guidance
Restore only the verified endpoint, listener or network configuration using the approved change process. Avoid broad public ingress rules as a shortcut. Verify DNS resolution, an application-side TCP connection and a database query. Record which controlled change improved reachability and keep a rollback plan.

retrieved_chunks.title: Application startup and migration failures
retrieved_chunks.text:
Application startup and migration failures
Scope: Services failing during initialization or schema migrations
## Symptoms
migration failed; startup failed; schema version mismatch; revision not found.

These are project-authored investigation notes, not an official diagnosis. Use the supplied logs to establish observed symptoms and cite their original line identifiers. Treat configuration changes, impact and the exact root cause as unknown unless evidence supports them. This runbook suggests checks; CloudLens never executes changes to the affected system.


## Diagnostic checks
Identify the first failing startup or migration step and preserve its trace. Compare deployed application version, migration files and current database revision. Confirm database reachability and access before investigating schema changes. Inspect whether another migration is active. A failed migration does not establish that a database rollback is safe. Collect the exact revision and failure details without exposing connection credentials.


## Missing evidence
Collect surrounding application logs, relevant deployment configuration, dependency-side evidence and a known-good comparison. Preserve timestamps when present and label absent timestamps as unknown. Record evidence that contradicts a proposed cause as well as evidence supporting it. If only a generic failure message is available, report insufficient evidence and request context rather than asserting a cause.


## Recovery guidance
Apply only an approved migration or rollback after checking backups, compatibility and whether the failed step partially changed data. Do not automatically downgrade a database from a generic startup error. Verify the expected schema revision, successful startup and representative read/write behavior under the application’s intended permissions.
